## Solution

**Answer:** $P(\{D_1, D_2, \dots\} = \mathbb{N}) = 1$.

**Proof.**

First, I check the problem statement for any leaked answers or solution sketches — none are present.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, define the event
$$A_k = \{k \text{ appears among } D_1, D_2, \dots\} = \bigcup_{n \ge k} \{D_n = k\}.$$
Note that $D_n$ can equal $k$ only when $n \ge k$ (since $D_n \in \{1,\dots,n\}$), and for $n \ge k$,
$$P(D_n = k) = \frac{1}{n}.$$
The random variables $D_1, D_2, \dots$ are independent, so the events $\{D_n = k\}$ for $n \ge k$ are independent. Therefore
$$P(A_k^c) = P\!\left(\bigcap_{n=k}^{\infty} \{D_n \ne k\}\right) = \prod_{n=k}^{\infty}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right) = \prod_{n=k}^{\infty} \frac{n-1}{n}.$$
The partial products telescope:
$$\prod_{n=k}^{N} \frac{n-1}{n} = \frac{k-1}{k}\cdot\frac{k}{k+1}\cdots\frac{N-1}{N} = \frac{k-1}{N} \xrightarrow{N\to\infty} 0.$$
Hence $P(A_k^c) = 0$, i.e., $P(A_k) = 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. (For $k=1$ this is immediate since $D_1 = 1$ always.)

Now observe that
$$\{D_1, D_2, \dots\} = \mathbb{N} \iff \bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k.$$
By the union bound,
$$P\!\left(\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k\right)^{\!c}\right) = P\!\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k^c\right) \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} P(A_k^c) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 0 = 0.$$
Therefore
$$P(\{D_1, D_2, \dots\} = \mathbb{N}) = P\!\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k\right) = 1. \qquad \blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
